nameStory: The laughing gull gets its delightful name from its distinctive call that sounds remarkably like human laughter - a loud, raucous "ha-ha-ha-ha" that echoes across coastal areas. When you hear a group of these birds together, it truly sounds like a beach party in full swing! This laugh-like vocalization is so characteristic that early naturalists couldn't resist giving them this cheerful common name.
description: The laughing gull is a medium-sized seabird that's perfectly at home along New England's coastline. These gulls are smaller than the familiar herring gulls you see at the beach, with sleek bodies built for agile flight and opportunistic feeding. Adults develop a striking black hood during breeding season that makes them easy to identify among other gulls. They're social birds that gather in large, noisy flocks and will eat almost anything - from fish and crabs to french fries and sandwich scraps.

idTips.label: Black Hood in Summer
idTips.description: During breeding season (spring through summer), adults sport a complete jet-black hood that covers the entire head and upper neck, creating a dramatic mask-like appearance that's unmistakable

idTips.label: Laughing Call
idTips.description: Listen for their signature "ha-ha-ha-ha" call that sounds exactly like human laughter - once you hear it, you'll never forget this raucous, carrying sound that's often heard before you see the bird

idTips.label: Wing Tips
idTips.description: In flight, look for solid black wing tips without the white spots that many other gulls have - the black extends well down the wing creating a bold, clean pattern

idTips.label: Red Bill and Legs
idTips.description: Adults have bright red-orange bills and legs that look almost plastic in their intensity - the bill is slightly drooped at the tip and feels smooth if handled

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller and more slender than the chunky herring gulls, with a more delicate build and quicker, more agile flight pattern

idTips.label: Winter Appearance
idTips.description: In fall and winter, the black hood is replaced by a white head with dark smudging around the eyes and behind the ears, giving them a somewhat disheveled look

habitat: Look for laughing gulls along New England's salt marshes, beaches, coastal ponds, and harbors, especially from Cape Cod southward where they're most common. They prefer areas where salt water meets fresh water, like estuaries and tidal creeks, and are often seen around fishing docks and seafood restaurants. These adaptable birds also frequent garbage dumps, parking lots near the coast, and anywhere humans gather with food.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin developing their striking black hoods in late March and April, making identification easiest. This is when they arrive at breeding colonies and their laughing calls become most frequent and noticeable.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification season when adults display full black hoods and bright red bills and legs. Young birds appear in late summer, looking mottled brown and lacking the distinctive adult features.
seasonality.fall: Adults begin losing their black hoods, showing patchy black and white heads during molt. Migration peaks in September and October when large flocks move through coastal areas.
seasonality.winter: Most laughing gulls migrate south, but some remain along the southern New England coast. Winter birds show white heads with dark ear patches and are much quieter than their boisterous summer selves.

funFact: Laughing gulls are such skilled opportunists that they've been observed following brown pelicans and actually stealing fish right out of the pelican's pouch as it surfaces from a dive - essentially using these much larger birds as their personal fishing service!
confusionNotes: In winter, laughing gulls can be confused with Bonaparte's gulls, but laughing gulls are larger, have thicker bills, and show dark smudging behind the eye rather than a neat black ear spot. Remember: "Laughing gulls look like they've been in a fight, Bonaparte's gulls look like they're wearing neat earmuffs."
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name suggesting constant merriment, laughing gulls are actually quite aggressive and will steal food from other birds, chase away competitors, and even engage in aerial battles over prime feeding spots. Their "laughter" is often more about territorial disputes than joy!
compareHints: Franklin's gull, the laughing gull's closest relative in the same genus, is extremely rare in New England and shows a distinctive white band separating the black wing tip from the gray wing. Laughing gulls lack this white band and have more extensive black on their wing tips. Franklin's gulls also have a more petite build and are typically found in prairie wetlands rather than coastal areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Franklin's Gull is much smaller and more compact than its closest New England relative, the Laughing Gull, with a noticeably shorter, thicker neck and smaller head.
